full_text_en:
Cheng Chunying v. Zhang Tao and PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited, Nanjing Branch — dispute over liability for motor vehicle traffic accident

**Ruling Summary**

If, during the term of an insurance contract, the degree of risk of the subject matter insured significantly increases, the insured shall promptly notify the insurer, who may increase the premium or terminate the contract. If the insured fails to give notice, the insurer shall not be liable for compensation for an insured event that occurs as a result of the significant increase in the degree of risk of the subject matter insured. A vehicle insured for household private use that is used for ride-hailing service operations significantly increases the degree of risk of the vehicle, and the insured shall promptly notify the insurance company. If the insured fails to give notice, the insurance company may be exempted from liability within the limits of the commercial third-party liability insurance for a traffic accident that occurs due to the operation of a ride-hailing service.

Plaintiff: Cheng Chunying, female, 34 years old, Han Chinese, residing in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Zhang Tao, male, 31 years old, Han Chinese, residing in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited, Nanjing Branch, domiciled at Longpan Middle Road, Xuanwu District, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Responsible person: Lou Weimin, General Manager of the Branch.

The plaintiff, Cheng Chunying, filed a lawsuit with the Jiangning District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, against the defendants, Zhang Tao and PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited, Nanjing Branch (hereinafter referred to as PICC Nanjing Branch), regarding a dispute over liability for a motor vehicle traffic accident.

The plaintiff, Cheng Chunying, alleged: On July 28, 2015, the defendant Zhang Tao, while driving a car, collided with an electric bicycle driven by the plaintiff Cheng Chunying, causing Cheng Chunying injuries and damage to the vehicle. According to an appraisal, the plaintiff suffered Class 9 and Class 10 disabilities. The car driven by defendant Zhang Tao was insured with defendant PICC Nanjing Branch under compulsory motor vehicle traffic accident liability insurance (hereinafter "CMLI") and commercial third-party liability insurance (hereinafter "commercial insurance"). The plaintiff requested that the two defendants compensate for medical expenses, nutrition expenses, disability compensation, etc., totaling RMB 255,339.75.

The defendant Zhang Tao argued: Zhang Tao was not at fault; the plaintiff Cheng Chunying should bear equal or greater responsibility. The car driven by Zhang Tao was insured with defendant PICC Nanjing Branch under CMLI and commercial insurance. Zhang Tao picked up passengers on the way home to share fuel costs, which did not constitute a commercial operation and did not significantly increase the risk of the vehicle; thus, PICC Nanjing Branch should compensate within the limits of CMLI and commercial insurance.

The defendant PICC Nanjing Branch argued: Defendant Zhang Tao was not at fault; the plaintiff Cheng Chunying should bear equal or greater responsibility. Zhang Tao used a vehicle insured for household private use for commercial operations, changed the vehicle's purpose, significantly increased the risk, and failed to notify PICC Nanjing Branch; therefore, PICC Nanjing Branch is exempt from liability under the commercial insurance.

The Jiangning District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, found at first instance:

On the afternoon of July 28, 2015, defendant Zhang Tao received an order for a ride-hailing service through a ride-hailing app. The order was to transport a passenger from NARI Group to the Evergrande Oasis residential area. Zhang Tao drove his own car to NARI Group to pick up the ride-hailing passenger. At approximately 5:05 p.m., Zhang Tao, driving the car carrying the ride-hailing passenger, was traveling west to east on Qianzhuang Road. When making a right turn south at the T-junction with Qingshuiting East Road, he collided with an electric bicycle driven by plaintiff Cheng Chunying, who was traveling north to south through the intersection on Qingshuiting East Road, causing Cheng Chunying injuries and damage to the vehicle. The Traffic Police Brigade of the Jiangning Branch of the Nanjing Municipal Public Security Bureau issued Road Traffic Accident Certificate No. Ning Gong Jiao Zheng Zi [2015] No. 0018, stating that it could not determine whether Cheng Chunying had complied with traffic signals.

The plaintiff Cheng Chunying was hospitalized for treatment. The hospital diagnosed her with acute closed severe traumatic brain injury. According to an appraisal, Cheng Chunying suffered mild mental impairment due to traumatic brain injury, with partial limitation of daily activities, constituting a Class 9 disability; a cranial defect of more than 6 square centimeters constituted a Class 10 disability; the period for lost work was 180 days, the nursing period was 90 days, and the nutrition period was 90 days. Upon review, it was confirmed that the plaintiff incurred the following losses due to the accident: medical expenses of RMB 99,122.26 (of which Zhang Tao paid RMB 59,321 and PICC Nanjing Branch paid RMB 10,000), hospital meal subsidies of RMB 560, nutrition expenses of RMB 1,350, lost wages of RMB 3,427.48, nursing expenses of RMB 7,650, disability compensation of RMB 156,126.60, mental distress damages of RMB 10,500, and transportation expenses of RMB 500, totaling RMB 279,236.34.

The nature of use listed on the vehicle registration certificate for the car driven by defendant Zhang Tao was "non-operational." On March 27, 2015, Zhang Tao insured the car with defendant PICC Nanjing Branch under CMLI and commercial insurance with a limit of RMB 1,000,000, with insurance periods from March 28, 2015, to March 27, 2016. The nature of use on the insurance policy was "household private car."

The Jiangning District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, held at first instance:

Citizens' right to health is protected by law. A person who infringes upon another's rights due to fault shall bear tort liability.

Regarding the allocation of responsibility for this traffic accident: Article 76 of the Road Traffic Safety Law of the People's Republic of China provides that where a motor vehicle traffic accident causes losses, the insurance company shall first compensate within the limits of CMLI. For any shortfall, if the accident occurs between a motor vehicle and a non-motor vehicle driver, and the non-motor vehicle driver is not at fault, the motor vehicle party shall bear compensation liability. If there is evidence that the non-motor vehicle driver was at fault, the compensation liability of the motor vehicle party shall be appropriately reduced based on the degree of fault. In this case, defendant Zhang Tao, while driving a motor vehicle, made a right turn, while plaintiff Cheng Chunying, driving a non-motor vehicle, was going straight. A turning vehicle should yield to a straight-going vehicle, and Zhang Tao failed to yield, constituting fault. The defendant failed to prove that plaintiff Cheng Chunying had committed any fault such as running a red light; therefore, Zhang Tao shall bear full liability for the accident. The losses incurred by Cheng Chunying due to the traffic accident shall first be compensated by defendant PICC Nanjing Branch within the CMLI limit, and any shortfall shall be compensated by the motor vehicle party.

Regarding whether defendant PICC Nanjing Branch should compensate under the commercial insurance: Article 52 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Insurance Law") provides: "If, during the term of an insurance contract, the degree of risk of the subject matter insured significantly increases, the insured shall, in accordance with the contract, promptly notify the insurer. The insurer may increase the premium or terminate the contract in accordance with the contract... If the insured fails to fulfill the notification obligation set forth in the preceding paragraph, the insurer shall not be liable for payment of insurance benefits for an insured event that occurs as a result of the significant increase in the degree of risk of the subject matter insured." An insurance contract is a bilateral contract where the premium and the insurance compensation are a quid pro quo. The insurer assesses the degree of risk based on the information provided by the insured to decide whether to underwrite and how much premium to charge. After the contract is concluded, if the degree of risk significantly increases, the probability of an insured event occurring exceeds the reasonable estimate made by the insurer at the time of contracting. If the insurer were still required to bear insurance liability according to the original contract terms, it would be manifestly unfair to the insurer.

In the current field of vehicle insurance, insurance companies classify insured vehicles into household private use and commercial operation based on their purpose and set different premium rates. The premium for commercial vehicles is nearly double that for household private vehicles. This is because, compared with household private vehicles, commercial vehicles have higher mileage, higher frequency of use, and naturally a higher probability of traffic accidents. This is both common knowledge and the insurer's estimation of risk. The risk level of the vehicle is in a quid pro quo relationship with the premium: low risk for household private vehicles corresponds to low premiums; high risk for commercial vehicles corresponds to high premiums. A vehicle insured under the name of household private use, when used for commercial activities, significantly increases the risk. The insured should promptly notify the insurance company, which may increase the premium or terminate the contract and refund the remaining premium. If the insured fails to notify the insurance company and demands compensation for accident losses caused by commercial activities, it is manifestly unfair.

The difference between commercial activities and household private use lies in: First, commercial activities are for the purpose of charging fees, while household private use generally does not involve charging fees. Second, the service object of commercial activities is unspecified persons who have no specific relationship with the vehicle owner; the service object of household private use is generally family members, friends, etc., who have a specific relationship with the vehicle owner. In this case, defendant Zhang Tao received the ride-hailing order through a ride-hailing app. He intended to charge a fee, and the passenger he carried had no specific relationship with him, which is consistent with the characteristics of commercial activities.

The commercial activity of defendant Zhang Tao significantly increased the risk of the insured vehicle. Zhang Tao should have promptly notified defendant PICC Nanjing Branch, which could have increased the premium or terminated the contract and refunded the remaining premium. Zhang Tao failed to fulfill the notification obligation, and his commercial activity caused the traffic accident in this case. Therefore, PICC Nanjing Branch is not liable for compensation under the commercial insurance.

In conclusion, in accordance with Article 48 of the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 76(1) of the Road Traffic Safety Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 52 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, the Jiangning District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, rendered the following judgment on December 14, 2016:

I. Defendant PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited, Nanjing Branch, shall compensate plaintiff Cheng Chunying RMB 110,000 within the CMLI liability limit, and defendant Zhang Tao shall compensate plaintiff Cheng Chunying RMB 99,915.34; both payments shall be made within ten days from the effective date of this judgment.

II. The remaining claims of plaintiff Cheng Chunying are dismissed.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, neither party filed an appeal within the statutory period, and the first-instance judgment has become legally effective.
